section.title: Consecration of the Priests
section.sectionRationale: Having described the priestly garments, God now gives the ritual for actually ordaining Aaron and his sons: washing, clothing, anointing, and a sequence of sacrifices that consecrate them and the altar itself, ending with God's own stated purpose for the whole tabernacle, that He may dwell among His people.
section.thesis: God prescribes a seven day ordination ritual of washing, clothing, blood, and sacrifice to consecrate Aaron and his sons as priests, and declares that through the tabernacle and its daily offerings He will dwell among the Israelites and be their God.
section.frameNote: Four movements: washing and clothing Aaron and his sons; the sin offering, burnt offering, and ordination ram with blood applied to ear, thumb, and toe; the seven days of atonement for the altar and the priests; and the daily offerings, ending in God's declared purpose to dwell among His people.

media.alt: Priests being washed at the tent entrance
media.caption: Aaron and his sons are washed and clothed before the Tent of Meeting.

verses.text: “Now this is what you are to do to consecrate Aaron and his sons to serve Me as priests: Take a young bull and two rams without blemish,
along with unleavened bread, unleavened cakes mixed with oil, and unleavened wafers anointed with oil. Make them out of fine wheat flour,
put them in a basket, and present them in the basket, along with the bull and the two rams.
Then present Aaron and his sons at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting and wash them with water.
Take the garments and clothe Aaron with the tunic, the robe of the ephod, the ephod itself, and the breastplate. Fasten the ephod on him with its woven waistband.
Put the turban on his head and attach the holy diadem to the turban.
Then take the anointing oil and anoint him by pouring it on his head.
Present his sons as well and clothe them with tunics.
Wrap the sashes around Aaron and his sons and tie headbands on them. The priesthood shall be theirs by a permanent statute. In this way you are to ordain Aaron and his sons.

units.label: The bull, and the two rams
units.note: blood on ear, thumb, and toe

verses.text: You are to present the bull at the front of the Tent of Meeting, and Aaron and his sons are to lay their hands on its head.
And you shall slaughter the bull before the LORD at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting.
Take some of the blood of the bull and put it on the horns of the altar with your finger; then pour out the rest of the blood at the base of the altar.
Take all the fat that covers the entrails and the lobe of the liver, and both kidneys with the fat on them, and burn them on the altar.
But burn the flesh of the bull and its hide and dung outside the camp; it is a sin offering.
Take one of the rams, and Aaron and his sons shall lay their hands on its head.
You are to slaughter the ram, take its blood, and sprinkle it on all sides of the altar.
Cut the ram into pieces, wash the entrails and legs, and place them with its head and other pieces.
Then burn the entire ram on the altar; it is a burnt offering to the LORD, a pleasing aroma, an offering made by fire to the LORD.
Take the second ram, and Aaron and his sons are to lay their hands on its head.

Slaughter the ram, take some of its blood, and put it on the right earlobes of Aaron and his sons, on the thumbs of their right hands, and on the big toes of their right feet. Sprinkle the remaining blood on all sides of the altar.

And take some of the blood on the altar and some of the anointing oil and sprinkle it on Aaron and his garments, as well as on his sons and their garments. Then he and his garments will be {{consecrated|consecrated}}, as well as his sons and their garments.

units.label: The ordination meal
units.note: eaten by Aaron and his sons alone

verses.text: Take the fat from the ram, the fat tail, the fat covering the entrails, the lobe of the liver, both kidneys with the fat on them, and the right thigh, since this is a ram for ordination,
along with one loaf of bread, one cake of bread made with oil, and one wafer from the basket of unleavened bread that is before the LORD.
Put all these in the hands of Aaron and his sons and wave them before the LORD as a wave offering.
Then take them from their hands and burn them on the altar atop the burnt offering as a pleasing aroma before the LORD; it is an offering made by fire to the LORD.
Take the breast of the ram of Aaron's ordination and wave it before the LORD as a wave offering, and it will be your portion.
Consecrate for Aaron and his sons the breast of the wave offering that is waved and the thigh of the heave offering that is lifted up from the ram of ordination.
This will belong to Aaron and his sons as a regular portion from the Israelites, for it is the heave offering the Israelites will make to the LORD from their peace offerings.
The holy garments that belong to Aaron will belong to his sons after him, so they can be anointed and ordained in them.
The son who succeeds him as priest and enters the Tent of Meeting to minister in the Holy Place must wear them for seven days.
You are to take the ram of ordination and boil its flesh in a holy place.
At the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, Aaron and his sons are to eat the meat of the ram and the bread that is in the basket.
They must eat those things by which {{atonement|atonement}} was made for their ordination and consecration. But no outsider may eat them, because these things are sacred.
And if any of the meat of ordination or any bread is left until the morning, you are to burn up the remainder. It must not be eaten, because it is sacred.

units.label: Seven days, and the daily offering
units.note: so that I might dwell among them

media.alt: A tent glowing with light at its entrance
media.caption: God declares He will dwell among the Israelites and be their God.

verses.text: This is what you are to do for Aaron and his sons based on all that I have commanded you, taking seven days to ordain them.
Sacrifice a bull as a sin offering each day for atonement. Purify the altar by making atonement for it, and anoint it to consecrate it.
For seven days you shall make atonement for the altar and consecrate it. Then the altar will become most holy; whatever touches the altar will be holy.
This is what you are to offer regularly on the altar, each day: two lambs that are a year old.
Offer one lamb in the morning and the other at twilight.
With the first lamb offer a tenth of an ephah of fine flour, mixed with a quarter hin of oil from pressed olives, and a drink offering of a quarter hin of wine.
And offer the second lamb at twilight with the same grain offering and drink offering as in the morning, as a pleasing aroma, an offering made by fire to the LORD.
For the generations to come, this burnt offering shall be made regularly at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting before the LORD, where I will meet you to speak with you.
I will also meet with the Israelites there, and that place will be consecrated by My glory.
So I will consecrate the Tent of Meeting and the altar, and I will consecrate Aaron and his sons to serve Me as priests.
Then I will {{dwell|dwell}} among the Israelites and be their God.
And they will know that I am the LORD their God, who brought them out of the land of Egypt so that I might dwell among them. I am the LORD their God.”

consecrated.gloss: To consecrate, set apart as holy. The verb underlies the whole ordination ritual: Aaron, his sons, their garments, and even the altar itself are made qadash, set apart exclusively for God's service, no longer available for ordinary use.

atonement.gloss: To atone, to cover or make amends. Used repeatedly of blood applied to the altar and of the ordination sacrifices, this verb describes the removing of sin's barrier so that sinful priests and a sinful people could be received before a holy God.

dwell.gloss: To dwell, settle, or tabernacle. The same root behind mishkan, tabernacle. God's stated purpose for all this ordination and sacrifice is not distant ritual but that He may shakan, actually dwell, among His redeemed people as their God.

basic.context: God gives the exact ritual for ordaining Aaron and his sons as priests: washing, clothing, anointing, and a sequence of sacrifices, including blood applied to their ear, thumb, and toe, that consecrate them and even the altar itself. The chapter ends with God's own explanation of why: so that He may dwell among Israel and be their God.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a literal, historical ordination ritual for Israel's first priests, not a repeatable pattern for Christian ministry today. Its significance lies in what it reveals about atonement, consecration, and God's stated goal throughout, dwelling among His people, which the rest of Scripture develops and ultimately fulfills in Christ.
basic.originalLanguages: The whole ritual is built around qadash, to consecrate or set apart, and kaphar, to atone or cover sin, since sinful priests could not simply begin serving a holy God without both cleansing and covering. The final verses reveal the purpose behind it all: God will shakan, dwell, among His people, the same word behind mishkan, tabernacle.
basic.typology: Blood applied to ear, thumb, and toe consecrates the priest's whole self, hearing, doing, and walking, to God, anticipating the whole-life consecration believers now offer through Christ. The seven days of atonement for the altar point to the completeness and finality later found in Christ's single, sufficient sacrifice.
basic.christ: Where Aaron needed repeated washing, clothing, and blood applied to be made fit to serve, Jesus is the sinless High Priest who needed no such purification for Himself, Hebrews 7:26-27, and who consecrates believers by His own single sacrifice, Hebrews 10:10, 14.
basic.god: God's holiness demands an elaborate, costly process before sinful men can serve Him, yet the entire purpose of that process, repeated three times in the closing verses, is God's own desire to dwell among His people. Holiness and nearness are not in tension for God; His holiness is precisely what makes safe nearness possible.
basic.crossReferences: Hebrews 7:26-27 contrasts Christ's sinless high priesthood with priests who first had to offer for their own sins. Hebrews 10:10-14 says believers are sanctified through Christ's one offering. 1 Peter 2:5 calls believers a holy priesthood offering spiritual sacrifices.
basic.oneStory: God ordains Aaron's priesthood through blood, washing, and repeated atonement so that He might dwell among a redeemed but sinful people. That whole costly arrangement points forward to Christ, the perfect High Priest whose one sacrifice consecrates His people fully, so that God now dwells in them by His Spirit.

context.literary:
Chapter 29 is the second half of a pair. Chapter 28 described what the priests would wear; chapter 29 describes how they become priests. It still belongs to the first of the seven divine speeches of Exodus 25 to 31, and it closes that speech with the words toward which the whole tabernacle section has been moving.

The ritual unfolds in clear stages. The materials are gathered, verses 1 to 3. Aaron and his sons are washed, clothed and anointed, verses 4 to 9. Three animals are then offered in a fixed sequence: a bull as a sin offering, verses 10 to 14; a ram as a burnt offering, verses 15 to 18; and a second ram, 'the ram of ordination,' verses 19 to 28. A note about passing on the garments, verses 29 and 30, is followed by the ordination meal, verses 31 to 34, the seven days, verses 35 to 37, and the daily offering, verses 38 to 42.

The order of the sacrifices is theological. First sin is dealt with; then the whole animal ascends to God in dedication; then the priests share a meal from the altar. Purification, consecration and fellowship come in that order, and Leviticus 9:22 later keeps the same sequence: 'the sin offering, the burnt offering, and the peace offering.' Three times Aaron and his sons lay their hands on an animal's head, verses 10, 15 and 19, and three times the smoke is 'a pleasing aroma,' verses 18, 25 and 41.

The final paragraph changes voice. Throughout the chapter God tells Moses what 'you' are to do. In verses 43 to 46 God speaks of what 'I will' do: meet with Israel, consecrate the tent, the altar and the priests, dwell among them and be their God. Human obedience gives way to divine action. The chapter ends with a double 'I am the LORD their God,' verse 46, the recognition formula that echoed through the plagues, 'the Egyptians will know that I am the LORD,' Exodus 7:5 and 14:4. Now Israel will know Him not as the God who strikes Egypt but as the God who comes to live with them.
context.historical:
Moses carries out this chapter in Leviticus 8, where the narrative follows the instructions closely, and on the eighth day Aaron offers his first sacrifices and fire from the LORD consumes the offering, Leviticus 9:1 and 9:24. During the ordination Moses himself acts as priest. He slaughters, applies blood and waves the portions, and the breast of the ordination ram becomes his share, verse 26. Aaron's priesthood is conferred by another; he does not ordain himself.

The ordination lasted seven days, verse 35, and Leviticus 8:33-35 adds that the priests could not leave the entrance of the tent during that time 'so that you will not die.' Seven is the number of the creation week and of completeness; a new order of service is being established over a full cycle of days. Ezekiel's vision of the restored temple later prescribes seven days of atonement for its altar as well, Ezekiel 43:26.

The measures of the daily offering are domestic ones. A tenth of an ephah of flour was about two dry quarts, and a quarter hin of oil and of wine a little under a quart each, as the BSB footnotes explain. Every morning and every evening Israel gave God a lamb with bread, oil and wine, the elements of an ordinary meal. The evening offering is timed 'between the two evenings,' the literal Hebrew of verse 39, probably the late afternoon.

That daily rhythm shaped Israel's prayer for centuries. Elijah prayed at Carmel 'at the time of the evening sacrifice,' 1 Kings 18:36; Ezra rose to pray 'at the evening offering,' Ezra 9:5; Gabriel came to Daniel 'about the time of the evening sacrifice,' Daniel 9:21, when there was no temple standing. The same rite of blood on the right ear, thumb and toe reappears in only one other setting, the cleansing of a healed leper, Leviticus 14:14. The rite that set apart the priest also brought back the outcast.
context.canonical:
Leviticus 8 and 9 record the ordination itself, and Leviticus 10:1-3 follows immediately with the deaths of Nadab and Abihu for offering 'unauthorized fire,' God's comment being, 'To those who come near Me I will show My holiness.' Numbers 28:3-6 restates the daily lambs and calls them 'a regular burnt offering established at Mount Sinai.' Kings and prophets measure faithfulness by that offering. Ahaz kept the morning and evening offerings on a new altar of his own design, 2 Kings 16:15, and Daniel foresees a power that 'removed His daily sacrifice,' Daniel 8:11. Haggai 2:12 asks the priests whether holiness passes by touch, a question raised by verse 37.

The promise of verse 45 becomes one of Scripture's great refrains. 'I will make My dwelling place among you... I will walk among you and be your God, and you will be My people,' Leviticus 26:11-12. Ezekiel 37:27 repeats it for the restoration after exile. Jeremiah 31:33 joins it to a new covenant written on the heart.

The New Testament uses the chapter at several points. John 1:14 says the Word 'made His dwelling among us,' using a verb built on the word for tent. Paul applies Leviticus 26 to the church: 'we are the temple of the living God,' 2 Corinthians 6:16. Hebrews contrasts Aaron's need to offer 'first for his own sins' with the Son who 'sacrificed for sin once for all,' Hebrews 7:27, and it sets the priests who stand 'day after day' beside the Priest who offered one sacrifice and 'sat down,' Hebrews 10:11-12. Hebrews 13:11-13 takes the sin offering 'burned outside the camp' of verse 14 and applies it to Jesus, who 'suffered outside the city gate.' Revelation 1:5-6 describes the church as made 'priests to His God and Father' by Christ's blood, and Revelation 21:3 hears the words of verse 45 at the end of history: 'the dwelling place of God is with man.'

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel to understand that the men who would stand between them and God were sinners too. The first animal offered at the ordination is a sin offering for the priests themselves, and they lay their hands on its head before it dies, verse 10. Priesthood did not rest on Aaron's merit. It was conferred through atonement, received from the hand of another, and sustained by God's own act: 'I will consecrate Aaron and his sons,' verse 44.

He also wanted them to see that the whole elaborate system had a single goal. The chapter could have ended with regulations. Instead it ends with God's purpose stated three times: He will meet with Israel, He will dwell among them, and they will know Him as the God who brought them out of Egypt 'so that I might dwell among them,' verse 46. The exodus was not only rescue from slavery. It was rescue for communion.

Finally, the daily offering taught Israel to live by a rhythm of dependence. Every morning and every evening, for all generations, a lamb went up on the altar at the entrance where God promised to meet them, verse 42. Access to God was not a single event in Israel's past. It was renewed every day, and the nation's life was framed by it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The ordination ritual is prescribed for Aaron and for each high priest who succeeds him, verses 29 and 30, and the daily offering is prescribed 'for the generations to come,' verse 42. Both belong to the Levitical order that Hebrews describes as 'only a shadow of the good things to come,' Hebrews 10:1. Christians do not ordain ministers with blood or offer daily lambs, and the laying on of hands in the church, Acts 6:6, is a commissioning with prayer, not a rite of atonement.

What continues is the substance. Those who serve God must first be cleansed by Another, and believers now draw near 'having our hearts sprinkled to cleanse us from a guilty conscience and our bodies washed with pure water,' Hebrews 10:22. The whole person, hearing, acting and walking, belongs to God, Romans 12:1. And the daily rhythm of offering finds its counterpart in the call to 'continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise,' Hebrews 13:15, which many believers have kept in morning and evening prayer.

debates.question: Why is blood put on the right ear, thumb and big toe, verse 20?

views.label: The whole person consecrated
views.case: The three points run from the top of the body to the bottom and stand for hearing, doing and walking. The priest must listen to God's word, serve with his hands and walk in God's ways. The sprinkling of blood and oil on the priests and their garments in verse 21 supports the idea that the entire person is being claimed.

views.label: A rite of passage into a new status
views.case: Others note that the only other use of the rite is the cleansing of a leper, Leviticus 14:14, where it restores an excluded person to the community and to worship. On this view the extremities mark a person crossing a boundary, from outside to inside or from common to holy, and the emphasis falls less on each body part than on the transition itself.

views.label: A detail left unexplained
views.case: A third group prefers not to assign meanings to each point, since the text gives none. It simply marks the priests with the ordination blood in a way that was visible and bodily.

debates.bearing: The first two views support each other: the rite marks a transition that claims the whole person. That the same rite ordains a priest and restores a leper is itself instructive; both are brought near to God by blood.

debates.question: What does 'whatever touches the altar will be holy' mean, verse 37?

views.label: Holiness is contagious
views.case: The altar becomes so holy that contact transfers its holiness, and whatever touches it now belongs to God. Leviticus 6:27 says the same of the sin offering's flesh, and Numbers 16:38 says the censers of the rebels 'have become holy' because they were presented before the LORD, so they were hammered onto the altar.

views.label: Only the holy may touch
views.case: Others read the verse as a restriction: whoever touches the altar must be holy, that is, only consecrated priests may approach it. Haggai 2:12 shows that holiness did not pass indefinitely from object to object, which suggests limits to any idea of contagion.

debates.bearing: Either way the altar, once atoned for and anointed, becomes a place of concentrated holiness that alters whatever comes into contact with it. The Gospels show a reversal of the direction of the uncleanness laws: Jesus 'reached out His hand and touched' a leper, Mark 1:41, and instead of becoming unclean He made the man clean.

debates.question: Does the sin offering take away the offerer's guilt, or purify the sanctuary?

views.label: An offering for the sinner
views.case: The traditional reading takes the chatta't as a sin offering that deals with the guilt of the offerer. Aaron and his sons lay their hands on the bull, verse 10, and Leviticus 9:7 says Aaron's sin offering was 'to make atonement for yourself and for the people.'

views.label: A purification of holy things
views.case: Many recent scholars prefer 'purification offering,' as the BSB footnote to verse 14 allows. They note that the blood is applied to the altar, not to the priests, verse 12, and that verse 36 speaks of purifying the altar 'by making atonement for it.' Sin pollutes the sanctuary, and the blood cleanses the place where God dwells so that He can remain.

debates.bearing: The chapter holds both ideas. The priests identify with the animal, and the blood goes on the altar. Sin affects both the sinner and the place of meeting, and Hebrews 9:22-23 says that 'nearly everything must be purified with blood' and that even 'the heavenly things themselves' required better sacrifices.

study.originalLanguages:
The verb translated 'ordain' in verses 9, 29, 33 and 35 is an idiom, mille' yad, literally 'to fill the hand.' The ram of verse 22 is the ram of millu'im, the 'filling.' The idiom is acted out in verse 24, where portions of the ram and bread are placed 'in the hands of Aaron and his sons' and waved before the LORD. The same idiom describes the Levites after the golden calf, 'Today you have been ordained,' Exodus 32:29, and a counterfeit priesthood when Micah 'ordained the Levite,' Judges 17:12, and Jeroboam 'ordained anyone who desired,' 1 Kings 13:33. The Greek Old Testament often renders the idiom with a verb meaning to complete or perfect, the verb Hebrews uses when it says the Son 'has been made perfect forever,' Hebrews 7:28.

'Lay their hands,' verses 10, 15 and 19, is samakh yad, to press or lean the hand. It is more than a touch. The offerer identifies himself with the animal that dies in his place. Leviticus 16:21 shows the fullest form, both hands laid on the goat's head while the high priest confesses Israel's sins over it. The same verb commissions Joshua, Numbers 27:23, which is why the gesture could later mean appointment as well as identification.

The 'sin offering' of verse 14 is chatta't, the ordinary Hebrew word for sin. The offering carries the name of what it deals with. The BSB footnote gives 'purification offering,' which captures the use of its blood to cleanse the altar, verses 12 and 36.

The 'burnt offering' of verse 18 is olah, from the verb 'alah, to go up. The entire animal ascends in smoke, and nothing returns to the worshipper. It is 'a pleasing aroma,' reach nichoach, a phrase first used when 'the LORD smelled the pleasing aroma' of Noah's sacrifice, Genesis 8:21. Nichoach comes from a root associated with rest and settling. Paul echoes the phrase when he says Christ gave Himself 'as a fragrant sacrificial offering to God,' Ephesians 5:2.

The word 'regularly' in verses 38 and 42 is tamid, continual. It describes the lamps that burn 'continually,' Leviticus 24:2, and the altar fire that 'must not be extinguished,' Leviticus 6:13. Later Hebrew uses hattamid, 'the continual,' as a name for the daily offering itself, and Daniel 8:11 speaks of a power that removes it.

Two more words anchor the chapter. 'Anoint' in verse 7 is mashach, the root of mashiach, the anointed one, first used of the high priest, 'the anointed priest,' Leviticus 4:3, before it is used of kings and of the Messiah. And 'meet' in verses 42 and 43 is from ya'ad, the root of mo'ed in 'Tent of Meeting.' The name of the tent is a promise: it is where God appoints to meet His people.

typology.type: Washing at the entrance of the tent, Exodus 29:4
typology.fulfillment: Before anything else the priests are washed with water at the door. The New Testament speaks of believers washed at the start of their service to God: saved 'through the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit,' Titus 3:5, and drawing near with 'our bodies washed with pure water,' Hebrews 10:22. Jesus tells Peter, 'Whoever has already bathed needs only to wash his feet,' John 13:10, echoing the pattern of a once-for-all washing followed by the daily washing of hands and feet at the basin, Exodus 30:19. The type falls short because water cleaned skin; Christ cleanses the conscience.

typology.type: The sin offering burned outside the camp, Exodus 29:14
typology.fulfillment: The flesh, hide and dung of the priests' sin offering could not be eaten or burned on the altar; it was carried outside the camp, the place of the unclean. Hebrews 13:11-12 draws the line directly: 'the bodies are burned outside the camp. And so Jesus also suffered outside the city gate, to sanctify the people by His own blood.' The escalation is that the one sent outside is not an animal but the Son, and the call follows, 'let us go to Him outside the camp, bearing the disgrace He bore,' Hebrews 13:13.

typology.type: The anointing oil poured on Aaron's head, Exodus 29:7
typology.fulfillment: Israel's law calls the high priest 'the anointed priest,' Leviticus 4:3. Jesus is the Anointed One in the fullest sense: 'God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power,' Acts 10:38, and He read Isaiah 61:1 as His own commission, Luke 4:18. Aaron's anointing was oil on the head for an office he would one day hand on; Christ's anointing is the Spirit given 'without limit,' John 3:34, for a priesthood He never relinquishes. His people share it, for 'you, however, have an anointing from the Holy One,' 1 John 2:20.

typology.type: The ordination meal that no outsider may eat, Exodus 29:33
typology.fulfillment: The priests alone ate the meat and bread 'by which atonement was made for their ordination,' and 'no outsider may eat them.' Hebrews 13:10 turns the rule around: 'We have an altar from which those who serve at the tabernacle have no right to eat.' Those who were once outsiders to Aaron's priesthood now feed on Christ, and those who cling to the old order stand outside. The type falls short in that Aaron's meal lasted seven days and was burned by morning, verse 34; the fellowship Christ gives does not run out.

typology.type: The daily lambs, morning and evening, Exodus 29:38-42
typology.fulfillment: Every day for generations two lambs went up on the altar, and the priests stood 'day after day' to offer 'the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins,' Hebrews 10:11. John the Baptist points to Jesus and says, 'Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world,' John 1:29. The escalation is from repetition to finality: 'this Priest had offered for all time one sacrifice for sins' and 'sat down,' Hebrews 10:12. The tabernacle's furnishings included no seat for a priest, because his work was never finished.

study.christ:
The ordination of Aaron opens with a sin offering for Aaron. That is the first contrast Hebrews draws: Jesus 'does not need to offer daily sacrifices, first for His own sins and then for the sins of the people,' Hebrews 7:27. He is 'holy, innocent, undefiled,' Hebrews 7:26. Where Aaron's hands pressed on a bull that died for his sin, Christ's hands were pierced for the sin of others, John 20:27.

The chapter's language of ordination reaches Christ in a remarkable way. The Hebrew idiom for ordination, filling the hand, was rendered in the Greek Old Testament by a verb meaning to make complete, and Hebrews uses that verb of the Son, appointed by an oath and 'made perfect forever,' Hebrews 7:28. His ordination was not a week of rites at the tent door but a life of obedience ending in the cross: 'He learned obedience from what He suffered. And having been made perfect, He became the source of eternal salvation,' Hebrews 5:8-9.

Jesus also consecrates Himself. In His prayer before the cross He says, 'For them I sanctify Myself, so that they too may be sanctified by the truth,' John 17:19. Aaron was consecrated by Moses; Christ sets Himself apart for His priestly offering and in doing so consecrates His people. Hebrews says we have been sanctified 'through the sacrifice of the body of Jesus Christ once for all,' Hebrews 10:10, and that 'by a single offering He has made perfect for all time those who are being sanctified,' Hebrews 10:14.

The sin offering carried outside the camp, verse 14, finds its place at Golgotha: Jesus 'suffered outside the city gate,' Hebrews 13:12. And the goal of the chapter, 'I will dwell among the Israelites,' verse 45, is met in the incarnation: 'The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us. We have seen His glory,' John 1:14. The glory that would consecrate the tent, verse 43, is now seen in a person. Jesus speaks of 'the temple of His body,' John 2:21.

The daily lambs belong here too. John's first public words about Jesus are 'Look, the Lamb of God,' John 1:29. The morning and evening lambs were never meant to be the last word; they were a daily reminder that sin required a death and that the death had not yet been sufficient.

There are limits to the pattern. The chapter's baskets of bread, the fat tail and the heave offering are not given a Christological meaning in the New Testament, and reading each detail as a picture of Christ would outrun the text. What the New Testament does claim is enough: Christ is the sinless priest, the perfected Son, the sacrifice outside the camp, the Lamb of the continual offering, and God dwelling with His people. Through His blood the church itself is ordained, made 'a kingdom, priests to His God and Father,' Revelation 1:6.
study.god:
The chapter's last paragraph turns the spotlight from Moses to God. Up to verse 42 God tells Moses what to do. From verse 43 He says what He will do: meet, consecrate, dwell, be their God. The priests are ordained by Moses' hands, but 'I will consecrate Aaron and his sons,' verse 44. Holiness is not produced by ritual technique. It is conferred by the God who is holy, and the tent is 'consecrated by My glory,' verse 43.

He is a God who purposes to live with His people. Verse 46 gives the reason for the exodus in a way that is easy to miss: He brought them out of Egypt 'so that I might dwell among them.' Redemption was not an end in itself. God freed Israel so that He could be at home with them. The same desire runs back to the garden, where the LORD God walked, Genesis 3:8, and forward to the new creation, Revelation 21:3.

He is holy in a way that sin cannot simply ignore. Even the altar, a thing of wood and bronze, needs atonement for seven days before it is fit, verses 36 and 37. Sin affects not only persons but the place where God meets them. The priests themselves need a sin offering. No one approaches on their own merit, not even those whose job is to approach.

He is also generous. The chapter is full of food. God gives the priests the breast and thigh as 'a regular portion from the Israelites,' verse 28, and He sets a meal before them at the entrance of His tent, verse 32. The one who demands holiness feeds those He calls to serve.

He is constant. The daily lambs are offered every morning and every evening, 'for the generations to come,' verse 42. God's meeting with His people is not occasional. He appoints a place and a time and keeps them without fail.

And He wants to be known. 'They will know that I am the LORD their God,' verse 46. In the plagues Egypt learned His name through judgment. Israel is to learn it through His presence. This shapes worship. We come not to a God who must be coaxed into nearness, but to one who has planned it, paid for it, and promised it.

crossReferences.note: The ordination of this chapter carried out: Moses presents 'the ram of ordination,' Aaron and his sons lay hands on it, and its blood is put on the right earlobe, thumb and big toe of each. The narrative confirms the instructions were followed exactly and shows the rite in action.

The priests must stay at the entrance of the tent for seven days 'until the days of your ordination are complete,' and keep the LORD's charge 'so that you will not die.' It fills out the seven days of Exodus 29:35 and shows how serious the ordination week was.

On the eighth day Aaron offers the sin offering, burnt offering and peace offering in the order set in Exodus 29, blesses the people, and 'the glory of the LORD appeared.' Fire comes from the LORD and consumes the offering, God's own answer to the promise of Exodus 29:43.

Blood is put on the right earlobe, thumb and big toe of a healed leper, the same rite used to ordain the priests in Exodus 29:20. The man excluded as unclean is brought back by the same sign that brought the priests near.

The daily lambs of Exodus 29:38-42 are restated for the whole calendar of Israel's offerings and called 'a regular burnt offering established at Mount Sinai.' Every other festival sacrifice was added on top of this continual base.

The covenant promise behind Exodus 29:45: 'I will make My dwelling place among you... I will walk among you and be your God, and you will be My people.' The goal of the tabernacle is stated as the blessing of an obedient covenant people.

Christ does not need to offer first for His own sins, as Aaron did with the bull of Exodus 29:10-14. The law appoints weak men as high priests, but the oath appoints 'the Son, who has been made perfect forever,' the true completion of the ordination.

Priests stand day after day offering sacrifices that cannot take away sins, like the daily lambs of Exodus 29:38-42. Christ offered one sacrifice for all time and sat down at God's right hand, His work finished.

The sin offering burned outside the camp, Exodus 29:14, becomes the picture of Jesus suffering outside the city gate to sanctify His people. Believers are called to go out to Him and share His disgrace, and they eat from an altar the old priesthood cannot share.

The Word 'made His dwelling among us,' and 'we have seen His glory.' The promise of Exodus 29:43-45, glory consecrating the tent and God dwelling among Israel, is fulfilled when God takes flesh and lives among His people in the Son.

Paul applies the dwelling promise to the church: 'we are the temple of the living God,' and God says, 'I will dwell with them and walk among them.' What Exodus 29:45 promised through a tent is now true of a people indwelt by the Spirit.

The last echo of Exodus 29:45-46: 'the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them.' The purpose God announced at Sinai, to live among His people as their God, is the final word of the whole story.

study.oneStory:
From the beginning God meant to live with the people He made. In the garden the LORD God was 'walking in the garden in the breeze of the day,' Genesis 3:8, until sin sent the man and woman into hiding and then into exile. Exodus 29:46 names the answer God has been working toward ever since: He brought Israel out of Egypt 'so that I might dwell among them.' The exodus is a road back to the presence lost in Eden.

The chapter shows what that road requires. Sinful people, even the best of them, need washing, covering, blood and a mediator before God can live among them without consuming them. The seven days and the daily lambs show that the arrangement is real but incomplete; it has to be renewed without end.

The story after this chapter proves the point. Within a few chapters Israel has made a golden calf and God says, 'I will not go with you,' Exodus 33:3, until Moses intercedes. The glory does fill the tabernacle, Exodus 40:34, and later Solomon's temple, 1 Kings 8:10-11. But the priesthood falters, and in Ezekiel's vision the glory of the LORD 'moved away from the threshold of the temple,' Ezekiel 10:18. The prophet also sees it return, Ezekiel 43:4-5, and hears God promise, 'My dwelling place will be with them,' Ezekiel 37:27.

The promise is kept in Jesus. The Word made His dwelling among us, John 1:14. He is the sinless priest who needs no offering for Himself, the sacrifice burned outside the camp, and the Lamb whose one offering ends the daily repetition. Through His blood the Spirit now dwells in His people, and the church is called 'the temple of the living God,' 2 Corinthians 6:16, a whole people ordained as priests, Revelation 1:6.

The new creation completes Exodus 29 on a cosmic scale. 'Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them. They will be His people, and God Himself will be with them as their God,' Revelation 21:3. The words of verse 45 become the description of the world itself. John saw 'no temple in the city, because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple,' Revelation 21:22. The whole city has become the place where God and His people meet.

quiz.q: What was done to Aaron and his sons before they were clothed with the priestly garments?

options.text: They were washed with water at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting.
options.note: Verse 4 describes this washing as the first step of the ordination.

options.text: They fasted for seven days beforehand.
options.note: The chapter describes washing as the preparatory step, not a preceding fast.

options.text: They were anointed before being washed.
options.note: The order given is washing first, then clothing, then anointing, not anointing before washing.

options.text: No preparatory act is described.
options.note: Verse 4 explicitly describes washing them with water first.

quiz.q: Where was the blood of the second ram applied to Aaron and his sons?

options.text: On their right earlobes, the thumbs of their right hands, and the big toes of their right feet.
options.note: Verse 20 specifies this exact application of blood.

options.text: Only on their foreheads.
options.note: The forehead held the gold plate reading Holy to the LORD, chapter 28; the ordination blood went on ear, thumb, and toe.

options.text: On their hands only.
options.note: The blood was applied to ear, thumb, and toe together, not the hands alone.

options.text: No blood was applied to their bodies.
options.note: Verse 20 explicitly describes blood applied to ear, thumb, and toe.

quiz.q: Who was permitted to eat the ordination ram and the bread from the basket?

options.text: Aaron and his sons alone, since these things were sacred.
options.note: Verses 32 to 33 restrict this meal to Aaron and his sons, forbidding any outsider.

options.text: Any Israelite who wished to participate.
options.note: Verse 33 explicitly states no outsider may eat these sacred things.

options.text: Only the seventy elders of Israel.
options.note: The meal was restricted specifically to Aaron and his sons, not the broader group of elders.

options.text: The meat and bread were burned entirely, with no one eating.
options.note: Verse 32 explicitly commands Aaron and his sons to eat the meat and bread.

quiz.q: How many days were required to complete the consecration of the altar?

options.text: Seven days, with a bull offered as a sin offering each day.
options.note: Verses 36 to 37 specify this seven day process for consecrating the altar.

options.text: One day only.
options.note: The text specifically requires seven days of ongoing atonement, not a single day.

options.text: Forty days, matching Moses' time on the mountain.
options.note: Forty days describes Moses' time on Sinai in chapter 24, not the altar's consecration period here.

options.text: No specific number of days is given.
options.note: Verse 37 explicitly specifies seven days.

quiz.q: What did God declare as His ultimate purpose for the tabernacle and its ordained priests, according to verses 45 to 46?

options.text: That He would dwell among the Israelites and be their God.
options.note: Verses 45 to 46 state this explicitly as God's stated purpose.

options.text: That Israel would become a wealthy trading nation.
options.note: No such economic purpose is given; the stated purpose is God's dwelling presence among His people.

options.text: That the priesthood would rule Israel as kings.
options.note: The priesthood served a ministering role before God, not a governing, kingly role over the nation.

options.text: No purpose is stated for the tabernacle.
options.note: Verses 45 to 46 explicitly state God's purpose to dwell among His people.

questions: Aaron could not simply step into priestly service; he had to be washed, clothed, and covered with blood first. Where in your own life have you tried to serve God without first receiving the cleansing and covering He provides in Christ?

Blood was applied to Aaron's ear, thumb, and toe, consecrating his whole self, what he heard, did, and where he walked. Which of these three areas of your life most needs to be brought under God's ownership this week?

The ordination meal was restricted to Aaron and his sons alone, a sacred and exclusive privilege. How do you currently treat the privilege of approaching God through Christ, casually or with the weight it deserves?

The chapter's real climax is God's declared purpose: 'that I may dwell among them.' How much of your view of your faith centers on rules and rituals versus centering on God's actual presence with you?

The altar itself needed seven days of atonement before it was fit for ongoing use. Where might you need patience with your own slow progress in holiness, trusting that God is still at work consecrating you over time?

translationNotes.note: In this way you are to ordain Aaron and his sons translates a Hebrew phrase literally meaning to fill the hand, an idiom for installing someone in office, likely originating from placing the priestly portion of the sacrifice directly into the ordinand's hands, as seen in verse 24.

Atonement was made for their ordination and consecration shows that even Aaron, the one who would later make atonement for others, first needed atonement made for himself, underscoring that no human priest, however honored, was without need of covering for sin.

I will dwell among the Israelites uses the same Hebrew root, shakan, that gives the tabernacle its name, mishkan, tying the entire chapter's ritual detail back to God's simple, central purpose of nearness to His people.
